exercises.title: Stop duplicate events
exercises.brief: A webhook can deliver the same event more than once. Keep only the first occurrence of each ID and preserve arrival order. IDs are strings; the input may be empty.
exercises.example: Input ["a", "b", "a"] should return ["a", "b"]. The starter returns ["a", "b", "a"].
exercises.extension: How would you bound memory if the service ran for months? Explain what happens when an old ID returns.

reference.explanation: The seen set was never updated. Add each accepted ID to it. Average time O(n), extra space O(u) for u unique IDs.
Insert each accepted ID into seen. The set was only read, so no duplicate was recognized. Average time O(n), extra space O(u).

exercises.title: Fix an expiring cache
exercises.brief: A value stored at time 10 with ttl 5 is valid before time 15 and missing at time 15. A missing key returns None in Python or nullopt in C++. Time increases, ttl is non-negative, and timestamp sums fit in the chosen integer type.
exercises.example: put("a", "value", 10, 5); get("a", 15) should be missing. The starter returns "value".
exercises.extension: Expired keys that are never read still occupy memory. Describe a cleanup strategy and its cost.

reference.explanation: Expiry is exclusive. Use >= so the exact boundary and zero TTL expire correctly. Lookup and insertion are average O(1). Lazy expiry alone does not bound memory.
Use >= for the exclusive expiry boundary. Return nullopt and erase the expired entry. Lookup is average O(1); explain cleanup for unread expired entries.

exercises.title: Reject a cyclic task plan
exercises.brief: Tasks depend on other tasks. Return any order where each dependency comes first. A cyclic plan must be rejected, rather than returning a partial result. Task IDs are unique and every dependency refers to a known task.
exercises.example: Tasks 0,1,2 with dependencies 0->1 and 1->0 must be rejected. The starter returns only task 2.
exercises.extension: An order can be valid without being unique. How would you choose a stable order, and what would it cost?

reference.explanation: Kahn’s algorithm processes only tasks whose remaining dependency count is zero. If fewer than all tasks are emitted, a cycle remains. Reject that partial result. Time and space O(V + E).
A cycle prevents some tasks from becoming ready. Compare emitted tasks with count and reject incomplete plans. Time and space O(V + E).
